overview.summary: Live health of the active namespace: identity supply, acquire and report rates, success and risk ratios, per-site cards, open breakers, low-watermark warnings and node activity.
steps: The window selector rescales the rates and ratios at the top; the two trend charts and the node table always cover the last hour.
The open-breaker and low-watermark cards name the endpoint groups that are refusing leases or running out of identities.
Each site card breaks its identities down by lifecycle state, so you can see which site is degrading.
overview.when: Crawlers suddenly return fewer results and you need to know whether identities, proxies or a tripped breaker are to blame.

identities.summary: Every credential the scheduler leases to crawler nodes, with its lifecycle state, health score and manual operations.
steps: Filter by site, identity type, state, tags, account or score range, then select rows.
Cooldown, ban, quarantine, expire, disable or archive the selection — and lift each of those again.
Import from JSON Lines or CSV, or revert the automatic actions a rule applied in a time range; reverted identities go back to pending.
identities.when: A rule banned a batch of cookies after a false captcha wave and you need them back in the pool.

identity-detail.summary: One identity: its state timeline, payload versions, live scheduler state per endpoint group and recent risk events.
steps: Edit region, tags, labels and the account reference without touching the payload.
Store a new payload version, or reveal the masked one — revealing needs identity:reveal and is audited.
Read the per-endpoint-group health scores and remaining cooldowns before operating on it.
identity-detail.when: One account keeps failing on a single endpoint group and you want to see whether its payload expired or the proxy is at fault.

identity-types.summary: The payload schema of each family of credentials on a site: fields, unique key, activation and the delivery mapping nodes receive.
steps: Describe the fields (string, number, bool, cookie_map, json, secret_ref) in YAML.
Preview how a lease delivers them: cookies, a cookie header, request headers, query parameters, a JSON body or plain values.
Saving creates the next version; the site cannot be changed afterwards.
identity-types.when: You start crawling a site with a new login flow and must define what one cookie record contains before importing any.

accounts.summary: Accounts group the identities of one site under a single external reference, so a ban or a disable applies to all of them at once.
steps: Filter by site, state or external reference, then ban, cooldown, disable or enable an account.
Every operation reports its outcome per member identity.
Identity imports create accounts automatically from the _account column.
accounts.when: An upstream account is flagged and every cookie derived from it must stop being leased immediately.

proxies.summary: The outbound proxy pool of the namespace: health, per-site state, provider comparison and manual operations.
steps: Import proxies as URL lines, JSON Lines or CSV; rows with the same URL are merged instead of duplicated.
Disable, ban, cooldown, quarantine or archive the selected proxies, or delete them outright.
The providers tab compares success and risk ratios per provider over the last hour, day or week.
proxies.when: One provider's exit nodes start returning captchas and you want to cool them down before they burn identities.

sites.summary: Sites, their client types, endpoint groups and URI rules — the structure every lease, cooldown and circuit breaker is scoped to.
steps: Create a site with its client types; every client gets a _default endpoint group.
Group URIs with similar risk behaviour and add the group's exact, template, prefix or regex rules.
The URI tester shows which group a request resolves to and which policies apply to it.
sites.when: A new API path behaves differently from the rest of the site and needs its own rotation and breaker settings.

policies.summary: The rotation, signal, action and breaker policies of the namespace, with drafts, published versions and bindings.
steps: Edit a policy in the form or in YAML, then publish it as a version.
Bind it to the namespace, a site, a client or an endpoint group; the most specific binding wins.
The resolve tab shows what actually applies where; the debugger replays a report against it before you publish.
policies.when: Captchas rise on one endpoint group and you want a stricter cooldown there without touching the rest of the namespace.

heatmap.summary: Identities × endpoint groups of one site client, coloured by remaining cooldown or by health score.
steps: Choose the site, the client and the metric, then read the grid column by column.
The state filter starts at active and pending; widen it to see banned, quarantined or expired identities — even “All” leaves out retired ones.
Click a cell to open that identity, or switch to the table view for the same data as text.
heatmap.when: Throughput dropped and you need to see whether a whole endpoint group is cooling down or only a handful of identities are.

breakers.summary: The circuit breakers of every endpoint group, the site switches, and the history of their transitions.
steps: Open a breaker for a fixed duration or indefinitely to refuse every lease of that group; closing it resumes them at once, without half-open probing.
Pause a whole site for an emergency stop — pausing is the one action that requires a reason.
Every open, close, pause and resume is written to the audit log, together with the reason you gave.
breakers.when: A site starts answering with bans and you must stop burning identities before the automatic breaker reacts.

config.summary: Versioned configuration distributed to crawler nodes: groups and keys, drafts, published versions and secret references.
steps: Edit the draft, validate it against the item's JSON Schema if it has one, then publish it as a version.
Compare any two versions and roll back to one of them.
Reference secrets as ${secret:path} instead of pasting values; the console keeps showing the reference, nodes receive the resolved value.
config.when: You change a signing parameter for the whole fleet and want it live within seconds, with a version to roll back to.

secrets.summary: The encrypted secret store of the namespace. Values are write-only in the console: nodes resolve them through their token, people need an audited reveal.
steps: Create a secret under a path such as signing/api_key, then reference it from config items as ${secret:signing/api_key}.

A node reads a value with its own token — directly through GetSecret, or by reading a config item whose references the server resolves for it. Either way the token's secret:read glob must cover the path, or the read is refused with scope_missing.
Revealing a plaintext in the console needs secret:reveal; allowed and denied attempts alike are recorded in the audit log.
secrets.when: A signing service key must reach every crawler node without ever appearing in a repository or a config file.

requests.summary: Every processed report stored in ClickHouse: outcome, blame, the matching rule, latency, identity, proxy and node.
steps: Narrow by site, endpoint group, outcome, identity, proxy, node or time range.
Read the summary strip for success, risk and latency percentiles.
Click a row to open the full event; without ClickHouse use risk events instead.
requests.when: You need the evidence behind a ban wave: which URIs, which proxies, and which rule classified them.

risk-events.summary: Non-success reports kept in PostgreSQL for the server's retention window (30 days by default) — available even when ClickHouse is not configured.
steps: Filter by site, endpoint group, outcome, identity, proxy, node and time range.
Expand a row for the request, its timings and its markers.
Blame says whether the identity, the proxy or both were faulted.
risk-events.when: A batch of identities was banned yesterday and you want to read the reports that triggered it.

notifications.summary: Where alerts of this tenant are delivered, and what happened to every alert that fired.
steps: Add a webhook, Feishu, DingTalk, WeCom or Telegram channel, for the whole tenant or for one namespace.
Limit a channel to certain alert kinds, sites and a minimum severity.
Send a test delivery, then watch the alert history for failed ones.
notifications.when: The on-call group chat should hear about an open breaker or a low identity watermark before your customers do.

tokens.summary: API tokens authenticate crawler nodes and automation. A token is bound to exactly one namespace and carries scopes: it may do what its scopes allow and nothing else, and every other call is refused with scope_missing.
steps: Give every node its own token and grant only the scopes its job needs — lease:acquire:<site>, report:write:<site>, config:read:<group>, secret:read:<namespace>/<path>.

Add secret:read only to nodes that must read secrets — directly through GetSecret, or because their config items carry ${secret:...} references the server resolves on their behalf; paths the token's glob does not cover are refused.
The token is shown once; add an IP allowlist, a rate limit and an expiry, and revoking it rejects its nodes immediately.
tokens.when: A new crawler fleet joins staging: it needs lease:acquire and report:write, plus secret:read only for the paths it actually reads.

users.summary: The members of this tenant and their role bindings. A user is a global account; a role binding is what grants it access here.
steps: A binding is a role plus an optional namespace and optional sites; without one the user sees nothing in this tenant.
viewer reads, operator operates, admin manages sites, publishing, secrets and tokens, owner also manages namespaces and users.
Extra permissions add one sensitive right — config:publish, secret:reveal, identity:reveal or policy:publish — without raising the role.
users.when: A contractor should operate identities in staging only, and never see production credentials.

audit.summary: Who did what in this tenant, whether it was allowed, and from which client — users, API tokens and the system itself.
steps: Filter by namespace, actor, action, resource or result within a time range.
Expand an entry for its payload, actor ID and user agent.
Turn on auto-refresh to follow activity live.
audit.when: A secret was revealed or a batch of identities was banned and you need to know who did it and when.

tenants.summary: A tenant is the isolation boundary of a team or organization; a namespace partitions one tenant into environments or business lines.
steps: Platform admins create tenants; owners create the namespaces inside them.
Creating a namespace also publishes the built-in default policies.
A namespace must be emptied before it can be deleted.
tenants.when: You separate production from staging, or onboard a second team that must never see your sites, proxies or credentials.

profile.summary: Your account as the server stores it, the tenant access your role bindings give you, and the console preferences of this browser.
steps: Language and theme are saved in this browser, not on the server.
Changing your password signs out all your other sessions.
Tenant access lists the tenants and namespaces your bindings cover.
profile.when: An administrator handed you an initial password and you want to replace it before doing anything else.
